note: A tree with invented joins in it is worse than no tree, so none of these has any. Each line is drawn in the form its own evidence supports.

rows.name: Booyzen
rows.depth: The Cape Dutch line the archive carries
rows.what: Graaff-Reinet, Cradock, Barkly East, then off the train at Johannesburg with nothing. The family changed one letter of its name in a war and kept the new spelling.

rows.name: Kolbe
rows.depth: London, 1802 — and a gravestone in the Karoo that agrees with it
rows.what: George Augustus Kolbe was born in Soho and sailed from Gravesend at sixteen, turning seventeen at sea. His stone at Burgersdorp gives 7 December 1802, and two hundred years later somebody found the London church book, which gives the same day.
rows.gap: No chart of this family has been drawn — only the pages that argue it.

rows.name: Barry
rows.depth: An Overberg merchant house, or a common surname — not settled
rows.what: The name recurs in the archive and the connection to the Overberg Barrys is suggestive and unproved. The archive says so rather than claiming it.
rows.gap: No chart, and no join established.

rows.name: The British women
rows.depth: Downing · van Jaarsveld · Mountjoy · Schoeman and the rest
rows.what: A Cape Dutch family that kept marrying British women. The lines that join it are the shape of the whole archive, not a footnote to it.

close: The form is checked, not asserted: a line counts as drawn only where this archive actually publishes a chart of it.
doors: 265 names — and none of them shared, which is unusual.
Including the sterfkennis forms the archive rests on.
